name: Logari

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A knowledgeable practitioner of Afghan folk dance.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: In the Logari style of Attan, dancers are known for rhythmic interruptions and spins, with musicians often adjusting the tempo to match the specific technique of the performers in the circle.
This is Logari. Traditional; documented in 20th-century ethnography.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (R_f8kKw_W7o)
Title card: Logari · Afghanistan · Traditional; documented in 20th-century ethnography

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Logari originates from the Logar Province of Afghanistan as a regional style of the Attan.
The Attan itself is a Pashtun dance with historical roots that some scholars associate with Zoroastrian religious ceremonies and ancient war dances intended to instill confidence in warriors.
on_screen: Map: Afghanistan · Central Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at formal and informal gatherings such as weddings, picnics, cultural events, and tribal meetings.
It is a symbol of celebration and regional identity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Delkash Dancing 1978 (https://archive.org/details/delkash-dancing-1978)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form a circle.
Movement includes full twists in place, arms held in the air, and bringing hands together medially to clap once or twice in the center.
The dance features rhythmic interruptions and spins.
Watch for Central Clap, Full Twist.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (R_f8kKw_W7o)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary instrument is the Dhol, a double-headed barrel drum.
The musician plays a critical role by tuning the beat to the technique of the performers.
Listen for the Dhol.
The music is driven by the Dhol, a double-headed barrel drum, which provides a consistent beat that can be adjusted in real-time by the musician to match the dancers' movements.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear traditional regalia.
Men often wear turbans, which are sometimes removed during the faster, final stages of the dance due to the physical intensity.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Logari is one of many styles of the Attan, including Kabuli, Wardaki, Paktiawal, Khostai, Shinwari, Khattak, and Mehsud.
A regional variant of the Attan, the national dance of Afghanistan.
